children: Heidi Overton, the Trump administration's nominee for FDA commissioner, repeatedly dodged questions about how she regards the president's often misleading or false claims about medical and health topics during a Senate hearing Thursday.
Overton, a physician who has served as deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy since 2025, was testifying before the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions.
When pressed by Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) if Trump was wrong when he made claims that the over-the-counter pain medicine Tylenol can cause autism, she evaded the question.

Hassan then asked if the president could ever be wrong. "As I've shared here before, I've had the privilege of working for the president for over a year and a half and have had robust discussions with him, along with all of his advisers," Overton responded.

Overton was also asked about Trump's major changes to the childhood vaccines schedule, a move that is contrary to decades of precedent that has been roundly criticized by public health experts. She was in the Oval Office in August when the president
an executive order making the changes.

Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) asked if splitting the MMR vaccine into separate jabs and cutting the recommended number of vaccines for children was the right move. "My job in my current role is to take the president’s directive [and] provide options to him," Overton replied.

The nominee did say that all vaccines currently marketed are "safe and effective according to the FDA," adding that the MMR vaccine is not deadly. Trump has previously stated that shot can be "lethal."
Overton also avoided a question from Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) regarding the safety of the prescription abortion pill mifepristone, saying that a safety review of the drug is ongoing.

title: FDA commissioner nominee Overton rebuffs questions about Trump medical claims
